item.title: US Air Force Cloud One platform breached amid wave of federal cyberattacks
item.description:
US Air Force Cloud One platform breached amid wave of federal cyberattacks

Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force’s Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department.

🔍 Overview

The intrusion was discovered within the past month during an upgrade of the cloud platform, disrupting application migrations and software updates. According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information. US Cyber Command has reportedly been called in to assess the impact, with the attackers, scope of the attack, and whether any data was stolen currently unknown. The Air Force declined to comment on the security or operational status of the affected systems, stating that it continuously takes measures to protect its information, systems, and mission capabilities.

⚙️ Key details

Cloud One is an enterprise cloud computing platform launched in 2017 and managed by the US Air Force. It allows Department of Defense agencies to host and manage applications supporting military operations, personnel management, logistics, and maintenance.

🛡️ Related Federal Breaches

On November 21, it was revealed that hackers reportedly breached the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies containing information on wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and other criminal justice records. This intrusion followed two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group breached FBI systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in the agency’s recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov.

Earlier this week, hackers also reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The incident also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). Hours after the CIA breach was reported, the US Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to its systems. It is unclear whether any of the recently disclosed federal government breaches are connected.

🧩 How it works

The CIA breach was reportedly conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing platform. ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that uses AI agents to automate various stages of a cyberattack, including discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, escalating privileges, and stealing data. The framework integrates with external AI models from Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, Grok, and others, allowing attackers to conduct autonomous attacks against organizations with minimal human intervention. According to the FBI, some ARTEX-powered intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

#USAirForce #CloudOne #ARTEX #FBI #Cyberattacks

Source: US Air Force cloud platform reportedly hacked in latest federal breach

item.title: AI Agents Fuel Large-Scale Cyberattacks on European Critical Infrastructure
item.description:
AI Agents Fuel Large-Scale Cyberattacks on European Critical Infrastructure

Recent alerts from Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies confirm that autonomous AI agents are conducting large‑scale attacks on critical‑infrastructure organisations, using publicly available frameworks to find and exploit vulnerabilities quickly.

🔍 Overview

  • Swiss NCSC: first reports of AI‑assisted attacks on Swiss organisations, including critical infrastructure across at least two sectors.
  • “In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said.
  • Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.
  • In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.
  • Italian CSIRT Italia: detected large‑scale campaigns using autonomous AI agents on exposed endpoints; observed multiple agents working in parallel; rapid attacks exploiting weak passwords and known vulnerabilities; AI chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, compromised credentials.
  • The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next.
  • In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours.
  • In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence.
  • Agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks.

🧩 How it Works

“During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low‑impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says.

“They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.”

⚙️ Key Details

Framework Involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents
ARTEX AI Yes
CyberStrikeAI Yes
DeepSeek Harness - Red Team Yes
PentAGI Yes
  • Reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet.
  • Prioritize patching, especially internet‑facing systems within 24 hours of release.
  • Add multi‑factor authentication (MFA) or passkey protection.
  • Enforce least‑privilege principles.
  • Disable remote management interfaces if not needed.
  • Monitor control‑plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic.
  • The number of publicly available AI agents has nearly doubled since October, fueling large waves of attacks.

💡 Why it Matters

  • AI agents can rapidly identify and exploit vulnerabilities across many systems.
  • They chain low‑impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains.
  • They can write malicious code in real time to evade defenses.
  • The attacks have already compromised IT systems in critical infrastructure.
  • Urgent mitigation is required to protect exposed assets.

#AIagents #Cybersecurity #CriticalInfrastructure #SwissNCSC #ItalianCSIRT

Source: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks

item.title: AI-Driven Cyberattacks Shift from Theory to Real-World Execution
item.description:
AI-Driven Cyberattacks Shift from Theory to Real-World Execution

AI-driven attacks are on the rise, transitioning from theoretical risks to real-world threats. Recent investigations reveal that criminals are using AI to accelerate attacks at scale, with attackers leveraging AI agents to execute context-aware commands with real-time decision-making.

🔍 Overview

In one observed campaign, a highly persistent threat actor utilized AI to generate 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed over 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days. This volume significantly exceeds the capabilities of normal attackers, who usually execute dozens of commands with a few scripts over similar periods.

⚙️ Key Details

The observed attack campaign featured two distinct phases, characterized by different execution styles:

Phase Characteristics Execution Metrics
Human Attacker Made typographical errors, repeated manual checks, demonstrated environment confusion Median time between commands roughly 24 seconds
Agentic Phase Flawless, zero-syntax-error commands Median gap between commands just 1.4 seconds

When instructed to execute aspects of an attack, the AI agent rapidly scans networks, attempts to elevate privileges, and utilizes legitimate native tools to blend in.

💡 Why It Matters

Attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates. If defenders wait hours to react, an AI agent can already have enumerated cloud infrastructure and extracted or encrypted data. To effectively defend against these threats, defenders must employ AI-powered tools.

Leveraging AI on the edge—specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW)—is a major strategic necessity. Edge-based AI can process telemetry instantly, making split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block active privilege escalation attempts locally. In observed product deployments, edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than the minutes required by agentic LLMs.

Furthermore, local edge AI maintains detection coverage even if an attack vector is used to temporarily disable network traffic to operate silently. This approach enables defenders to catch and isolate threats at the earliest possible stage and safeguards sensitive corporate data locally without requiring telemetry or proprietary data to be transmitted to the cloud for analysis.

🧩 Defense Strategy

Despite their speed, agentic AI attackers have a foundational weakness: they enter the environment without information. Defenders hold an upper hand through comprehensive AI analytics.

  • Data Normalization: Collecting telemetry across diverse network, endpoint, identity, and cloud sources to map distinct data streams into a single, cohesive schema.
  • Advanced Stitching: Merging related events across disparate sensors into unified, context-rich stories rather than disconnected events.
  • Baseline Establishment: AI analytics engines make it easier to create and update baselines.
  • Automated Response: Organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response capabilities, enabling instant attack isolation and automated remediation before critical systems or data are compromised.

#Cybersecurity #AIAgents #EdgeAI #ThreatDetection #NetworkSecurity

Source: The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense

item.title: New Extortion Group Inception Targets SSO Credentials; ShinyHunters Claims Return
item.description:
New Extortion Group Inception Targets SSO Credentials; ShinyHunters Claims Return

🕵️ Inception Targets Global Brands

A newly formed data extortion group named ‘Inception’ has been linked to a large-scale campaign targeting single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands. The gang surfaced on November 17, claiming seven victims on its extortion site, including chip maker AMD, PepsiCo, Cigna Healthcare, AutoZone, and Lucid Motors. However, none of these companies have publicly confirmed a data breach.

Cybersecurity company ReversingLabs has tracked the group’s activity since late October, identifying an extensive infrastructure that includes 21 domains used for SSO phishing, 41 domains believed to be part of the campaign infrastructure, and 4 other domains with suspected use. This infrastructure impersonates dozens of major corporations, including Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, Indeed, Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Twitch, Reddit, Nestlé, Anthropic, Nintendo, Starbucks, McDonald’s, Paramount, and NBCUniversal. The existence of these domains does not prove those firms have been breached or targeted yet.

⚙️ Tactics and Infrastructure

The Inception campaign appears to rely on phone-based social engineering rather than email phishing, strongly resembling tactics used by the ShinyHunters extortion group. The actors use legal-themed websites that imitate corporate authentication services, primarily Okta but also NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager.

Component Details
Phishing Domains 21 domains identified by ReversingLabs
Infrastructure Domains 41 domains believed to be used in the campaign
Suspected Domains 4 additional domains with suspected use
Impersonated Brands Includes Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, and Nintendo
Authentication Services Okta, NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager

Okta published a report linking Inception to threat cluster O-UNC-053, which was previously associated with ShinyHunters and active since March. According to Okta, after law enforcement disrupted ShinyHunters, O-UNC-053 continued to register new phishing domains. In late October, the cluster launched a legal-themed campaign, and in mid-November, the Inception leak site went live. Okta assessed that the cluster very likely changed its brand affiliation, maintaining consistent infrastructure and TTPs.

Inception responded to these links by claiming on its extortion page that it operates independently and has no affiliation to previous groups. The actors argued that overlapping targets and common domain registration services do not establish operational links, noting that private tooling circulates among independent threat actors.

📢 ShinyHunters Reemerges

Following a series of arrests targeting alleged ShinyHunters members, the group claimed to have returned on November 23 via a new Tor site. The site contains messages in Russian and English announcing the group’s return and distancing itself from alleged impostors. The operators denounced a former member, reportedly arrested and cooperating with law enforcement, and mocked other individuals tied to the investigation, including Umbreon and Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky.

To verify their identity, the new operators published two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys dating back to 2020. BleepingComputer confirmed that both messages were signed using known PGP keys associated with the group, indicating access to the private signing keys. However, these keys do not confirm that the individuals behind the new operation are the same people who previously controlled the group, as the keys have circulated among numerous people. The operators stated they plan to launch a new CDN for hosting stolen data and will communicate exclusively through a specific Exploit hacking forum account and the new Tor site.

🛡️ Defending Against the Threat

ReversingLabs recommends enforcing phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and strengthening help desk identity verification procedures to defend against the Inception campaign. Security teams should carefully review DNS, proxy, and identity provider logs dating back to October 21, 2026, for signs of suspicious activity.

#ShinyHunters #Inception #SSO #DataExtortion #Phishing #Okta

Source: New Inception extortion gang launches large-scale vishing campaign Source: ShinyHunters claims to return after FBI arrests, uses old PGP keys as proof

item.title: Analysis of 5,400 Malicious NPM Packages Reveals Evolving Supply Chain Tactics
item.description:
Analysis of 5,400 Malicious NPM Packages Reveals Evolving Supply Chain Tactics

In this first part, we analyzed approximately 5,400 confirmed malicious npm packages published between December 2025 and October 2026, the first year following npm’s revocation of long-lived authentication tokens. The dataset comprises packages detected by a scanner that analyzes npm publish events for suspicious packages, with results filtered for precision by retaining only packages with at least one independent source, such as a public advisory, a vendor-published campaign report, an npm security takedown, or analyst review. Time is measured by npm publish date, and the unit of record is the package version, dated by its first malicious version.

🔍 Threat Landscape Overview

Monthly counts of confirmed malicious packages vary by a factor of fifteen across the period. Activity remains stable with several hundred new publisher accounts per month and a flat rate of malicious packages relative to total packages published. In August 2026, a single dependency-confusion campaign accounts for 78% of confirmed versions. Dependency-confusion reconnaissance is continuous, present in every month at a consistent level, while compromise of legitimate packages is episodic.

🧩 Attack Vectors and Campaigns

Three waves of a single worm family occurred in May, June, and August 2026. The May and August waves each compromised more than one hundred packages, and the June wave republished a vendor’s entire scope in one day.

  • Token Theft Shift: Classic long-lived tokens were revoked on December 9, 2025. Theft of npm authentication tokens peaked at 22% of packages in March 2026 and fell below 5% from May. The tokens targeted in this period were plausibly granular access tokens and CI secrets.
  • Obfuscation: The share of actors whose packages trigger an obfuscation rule more than doubled between May and August 2026. 72% of packages have an obfuscation marker, and 30% retrieve a second stage.
  • Compromised Packages: 78% of compromised versions add or modify a lifecycle script, compared with 4% of attacker-created packages. 23% show a change of maintainer or publisher, but the majority of compromises are published through the legitimate account and leave ownership records unchanged.

⚙️ Attacker Profile and Package Characteristics

99% of malicious packages are published by single-maintainer accounts, and 55% of accounts use a free-mail address. Two-thirds of accounts publish exactly one malicious package; among those publishing more than one, the median interval from first to last malicious publish is under one day.

  • DPRK-nexus Campaigns: These are the exception, operating several hundred accounts at one to two packages each, with 83% on free-mail addresses.
  • Other Named Campaigns: These use free-mail addresses in 15% of cases, consistent with procured account pools.
  • Package Traits: 88% of packages are under thirty days old at the malicious publish, 75% declare no repository, and 65% retain npm init template values in the author, description, or repository fields. 54% declare a lifecycle script, and 17% carry an internal-looking name (core, utils, sdk, config). Typosquatting is a minority tactic, with 13% embedding a popular package name and under 5% being within two character edits of one.

💡 Payload Behavior and Targeting

Credential and data theft is the predominant behavior in every month, except August. In August, a significant number of packages stole credentials but ultimately aimed to deliver a Sliver command-and-control implant on the victim machine, changing their classification to Trojan / Downloader.

  • Credential Targets: 45% of credential stealers target a single credential class, while 36% target three or more. Single-class stealers are distributed evenly across cloud credentials, SSH keys, AI-developer credentials, npm tokens, and .env files. In multi-class stealers, cloud credentials, SSH keys, and .env files co-occur; wallet and browser-data theft occur separately.
  • AI Developer Credentials: Targeting remained at 1-4% of packages throughout the year, but absolute counts rose with volume. AI-developer credentials are the most specialized target: 80% of packages that target them target no other class.
  • OS Specificity: 55% of packages contain no operating-system-specific code. Droppers target Windows (PowerShell, scheduled tasks, executables), while credential stealers and backdoors target Linux (systemd, cron, shell configuration files). macOS-specific code appears in approximately one in eight stealers.
  • Scoped Packages: 24% of packages are scoped, across more than three hundred distinct scopes, most of which contain a single malicious package.

#npmSecurity #SupplyChainAttack #MalwareAnalysis #ThreatIntelligence #OpenSource

Source: What 5,400 Malicious npm Packages Reveal about Software Supply Chain Risk in 2026

item.title: Attackers Weaponize Autonomous AI Agents in 10 Global Campaigns
item.description:
Attackers Weaponize Autonomous AI Agents in 10 Global Campaigns

Attackers are weaponizing autonomous AI agents in real-world campaigns, creating a risk that until recently has only been theoretical. Between July and September 2026, more than 10 global campaigns were identified and tracked in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to enhance their attacks.

🔍 Overview

These agentic AI attackers operated at machine speed, compressing the attack lifecycle from weeks or days into mere hours. The campaigns targeted diverse sectors, including government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, and education.

In every observed campaign, attackers gained their initial foothold through web shells that were deployed via vulnerable web applications. The novelty of these agentic campaigns was not in their techniques, but in their speed and efficiency. The AI-driven operators matched the tradecraft of proficient human attackers while operating at machine scale, at times executing hundreds of unique commands in just minutes.

🧩 How It Works

An agentic AI attacker is an autonomous AI system—usually a large language model (LLM) with tool-calling capabilities—that independently plans, executes, and adapts attack sequences without continuous human guidance. Unlike chatbots that respond to individual prompts, agentic AI systems operate in a loop: they observe their environment, reason about what to do next, take action, and then observe the results to inform their next step.

The typical operational flow includes:

  • Human sets the objective: The human operator identifies a target and provides initial access, typically a web shell on a vulnerable web application.
  • AI agent takes over: The AI agent autonomously performs further reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
  • AI agent reports back: The AI agent structures its findings using machine-readable output formatting and periodically checks in with orchestration APIs.
  • Human makes strategic decisions: The human operator reviews the AI agent’s findings and directs high-level strategy, such as instructing the agent to target the payment system or establish persistence.
  • AI agent executes: The AI agent carries out the human’s strategic directives with tactical autonomy.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Speed and scale: An agentic AI attacker operates at machine speed. In the observed campaigns, AI agents executed hundreds of unique commands within minutes.
  • Lowered barrier to entry: Attackers can provide high-level guidance while the AI agent automates intricate technical phases, including compiling kernel exploits, navigating cross-platform lateral movement, and systematically compromising cloud infrastructure.
  • Adaptive reasoning: Unlike script-based attacks that fail when they encounter unexpected conditions, agentic AI attackers employ reasoning to try alternative approaches when failures occur. Agents were observed attempting five different privilege escalation techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed, and compiling custom exploit code on-target when pre-built binaries didn’t work.
  • Cross-domain fluency: A single agentic AI attacker can operate across Linux, Windows, various cloud platforms, web applications, databases, and network infrastructures.
  • Behavioral fingerprints: Using AI agents came at the expense of operational stealth. The agents left unmistakable behavioral fingerprints that revealed the involvement of non-human operators, including:
    • Structured machine-readable output formats.
    • Adaptive exploit selection.
    • Iterative refinement.
    • Chain-of-thought reasoning comments that appeared in shell commands.

💡 Why It Matters

New challenges in threat attribution have emerged because AI agents generate unique, dynamic payloads on the fly without distinct behavioral fingerprints, making it increasingly difficult to attribute attacks to specific threat actors.

Unit 42 AI Security Assessment service can help identify and mitigate complex AI-enabled risks. Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense is an offensive security service designed to assist organizations with continuously discovering hidden and unknown exposures in dynamic environments, validate real-world exploitability across attack paths through agentic testing and expert analysis, and provide prioritized remediation and virtual patching guidance to accelerate risk mitigation.

#Cybersecurity #AIAgents #ThreatIntelligence #PaloAltoNetworks #Unit42

Source: Recent Trends and Tactics of Agentic AI Attacks

item.title: European Commission confirms data breach via AI-assisted attack
item.description:
European Commission confirms data breach via AI-assisted attack

The European Commission has confirmed that attackers breached its EU Academy online learning hub and stole the personal data of an undisclosed number of users. This incident follows a disclosure that hackers breached the Commission’s systems on October 22 using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework.

🔍 Overview

  • The attack was conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework.
  • The breach affected the EU Academy platform, which is used to learn about EU policies and follow EU online courses.
  • The incident caused service disruptions that also affected the internal Sysper HR platform.
  • The Commission stated it has not detected evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.
  • No ransom demands have been received, and the attack has not yet been attributed to a specific actor.

🚨 Key details

  • Stolen data included users’ personal information, such as names and email addresses.
  • As a protective measure, the Commission temporarily took down several applications, most of which have since been restored.
  • Public access to the EU Academy platform has been disabled.
  • Users on the platform received a message warning them to be suspicious of unsolicited emails or messages that may be part of potential phishing attacks.
  • The investigation into the incident is still ongoing.

⚙️ Broader context

  • In February, the Commission disclosed a data breach after discovering on January 30 that a mobile device management platform used for staff devices had been compromised.
  • On March 27, the Commission disclosed an additional incident following a breach of its Amazon cloud environment.
  • The EU’s Cybersecurity Service (CERT-EU) attributed the March cloud hack to the TeamPCP threat group, noting it exposed the data of at least 29 other Union entities.
  • These incidents follow the Commission’s January 20 proposal for new cybersecurity legislation aimed at strengthening defenses against cybercrime groups and state-backed actors.

#EuropeanCommission #Cybersecurity #DataBreach #Artemis #AIHacking

Source: European Commission confirms data theft in EU Academy breach

item.title: Threat actors compromised 24 Check Point servers across 22 organizations in cyberespionage campaign
item.description:
Threat actors compromised 24 Check Point servers across 22 organizations in cyberespionage campaign

Threat actors exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise two dozen Check Point Security management servers in an ongoing campaign targeting 22 organizations, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. The activity, tracked as GT13, was confirmed as ongoing between October 17 and November 2, though researchers believe the campaign remains active given the threat actors’ persistent access to Check Point devices. The 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries and include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors.

🔍 Overview

The attackers launched their operations from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. GreyNoise detected the activity and noted it resembled cyberespionage operations, although the attacker’s motivation could not be conclusively determined. The researchers assessed that GT13 operated an AI-powered offensive tool, based on observed behavior, automation, and custom tooling, but this use of AI in the campaign remains unconfirmed.

🧩 How it works

The attack chain began with unknown means of initial compromise, though GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached. During post-compromise stages, the researchers observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232, an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments.

⚙️ Key details

The attackers leveraged automation and custom tooling, observed across more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 file-related activities. Their activities included:

  • Stealing firewall databases, credentials, configuration data, and internal certificate authority files
  • Generating a new certificate in one victim’s environment
  • Unloading security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections
  • Conducting internal network reconnaissance and attempting lateral movement

On October 26, the attacker performed a bulk certificate management operation across all 24 compromised Check Point servers, which failed, but still helped GreyNoise identify victims. The researchers also observed attempts to exploit multiple additional vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF), and CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script).

The campaign targeted additional enterprise systems including:

System Vulnerability Notes
Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-4966 Targeted in lateral movement
Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2024-21893 Targeted during campaign
VMware vCenter CVE-2021-21972, CVE-2023-34048 Multiple vulnerabilities exploited
Microsoft Exchange CVE-2021-26855/34473 Targeted during intrusions
Microsoft Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 Part of lateral movement attempts

BleepingComputer has contacted Check Point to ask if they have better visibility into those attacks and which flaw was exploited for initial access, and we are waiting for their response.

💡 Why it matters

Although GreyNoise lost visibility into the campaign operations on November 2, the researchers believe it could still be ongoing. The company has notified international government partners and CERTs to alert impacted organizations and shared indicators of compromise (IoCs) that could help identify additional intrusions or block future attempts. Check Point warned about CVE-2026-16232 in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

The campaign demonstrates sophisticated attack capabilities using compromised infrastructure and automation tools to conduct large-scale credential theft and lateral movement across critical infrastructure sectors including government, finance, and energy.

#cybersecurity #CheckPoint #GreyNoise #GT13 #cyberespionage #AI

Source: Hackers compromise Check Point Servers in 22 organizations

item.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence details AI agent hack on universities
item.description:
Amazon Threat Intelligence details AI agent hack on universities

Amazon Threat Intelligence shared findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor who used autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The investigation revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over a 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

🔍 Overview

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet. This visibility included project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

🧩 How it works

Cairn is built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple: given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. The actor in this campaign gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” Based on a list of targeted IP addresses and that goal, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

⚙️ Key details

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server.

Operation Target Duration Key Actions
Redis instance at one university ~16 hours 148 sequential actions; abused replication feature, escaped scripting sandbox, wrote to config files, corrupted memory, attempted Log4Shell injection
University GPU server > 6 hours Researched public presence to build list of ~80 usernames; tested > 30,000 credential combinations against SSH, admin dashboard, network storage, VPN, and campus portal
Open-source medical imaging AI application Not specified Identified framework, mapped API endpoints, found upload endpoint with a filename parameter

In the Redis operation, when initial attempts to take control failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded. In the GPU server operation, the agents never found a working login. Against the medical imaging application, the agents successfully identified the framework and mapped its API endpoints.

💡 Why it matters

These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening. Defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable, as the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction, even when specific operations did not succeed.

#Cybersecurity #AIAgents #ThreatIntelligence #Amazon #Zero-day #AutonomousHacking

Source: Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Chinese-linked actors misuse AI pentesting tool Cairn to exploit MONAI Label zero-day
item.description:
Chinese-linked actors misuse AI pentesting tool Cairn to exploit MONAI Label zero-day

In early September 2026, a Chinese‑nexus threat actor used the autonomous AI‑agent platform Cairn to discover and exploit a path‑traversal zero‑day in the open‑source medical‑imaging application MONAI Label, gaining root control of targeted servers.

🔍 Overview

  • Campaign observed between September 8‑10 2026.
  • Attributed with moderate confidence to a Chinese‑nexus threat actor.
  • Primary targets were East Asian educational institutions outside China.
  • Attack leveraged the autonomous AI‑agent platform “Cairn”.

🧩 How it works

  • Operators instructed Cairn agents to “obtain shell access”.
  • Agents autonomously discovered a path‑traversal zero‑day in MONAI Label.
  • Within 11 minutes they mapped the API, wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py, and triggered an endpoint to gain root.
  • After the initial compromise, operators supplied a proxy to a second university network running the same vulnerable software for further targeting.

⚙️ Key details

  • Cairn is a legitimate pentesting tool designed to coordinate multiple AI agents for research and defense.
  • The attackers left their Cairn instance publicly accessible without authentication, exposing the operation.
  • A 16‑hour, 148‑action attempt to take over a Redis server failed.
  • A separate six‑hour attempt on a university GPU server tried >30 000 credential combos and also failed.
  • Amazon Threat Intelligence shared two IP addresses used in the campaign: 142.4.98.145 and 142.4.107.34.
  • MONAI Label maintainers issued a security update on November 18 2026 after being notified.

📈 Impact

  • Successful compromise gave complete root control of a medical‑imaging server.
  • Similar Cairn abuse was documented in a large‑scale credit‑card stealing operation (Gambit Security) and in an attack on a U.S. aerospace organization (Google).
  • Amazon warned that AI agents can find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than manual security investigations.

🛡️ Mitigation

  • Apply the November 18 2026 MONAI Label security update.
  • Monitor for publicly exposed Cairn instances.
  • Adopt automated defensive measures to keep pace with AI‑driven attacks.

#Cairn #AIAgents #ZeroDay #Cybersecurity

Source: Hackers use autonomous AI tool Cairn to find zero-day, take over server

item.title: Unit 42 tracks Com-affiliated vishing and data extortion campaigns
item.description:
Unit 42 tracks Com-affiliated vishing and data extortion campaigns

Unit 42 has tracked and responded to numerous waves of vishing attacks conducted by Com-affiliated threat actors in recent months, leading to data theft and extortion attempts. Since early 2026, the team has attributed multiple data theft and extortion attempts to Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors.

🔍 Overview

  • The attacks have targeted data-rich industries, such as financial services, healthcare, and legal services.
  • Targeted organizations were primarily located in the U.S., UK, and Australia.
  • Attackers use the threat group and activity cluster naming conventions tracked by Unit 42.

🧩 How it works

  • Initial Access: Attackers establish access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization.
  • MFA Bypass: These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time.
  • Persistence: In multiple instances, attackers have enrolled an unauthorized MFA device within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence.
  • Exfiltration: Attackers have automated data exfiltration using Python scripts to target Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint content.
  • Extortion: Following exfiltration, attackers have sent Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees, claiming data theft and directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

⚙️ Key details

  • CL-CRI-1264: Identified in September 2026, this activity cluster primarily targets healthcare, pharmaceutical, and other medical organizations. Attackers targeted employees on both corporate workstations and personal mobile devices, reusing a single device named “Pixel 10a” across compromised accounts.
  • CL-CRI-1274: Also identified in September 2026, this cluster avoided re-prompting for Duo MFA by replaying a persistent “keep me signed in” session token. They then used scripted access through python-requests and the Microsoft Graph SDK to collect and exfiltrate data from SharePoint and OneDrive environments. Extortion messages were sent internally via email and Microsoft Teams.
  • CL-CRI-1192: During an investigation attributed to this cluster (which Google tracks under UNC6671), a malicious browser extension named “Google Chrome” (manifest version 1.6.111) was identified. The extension was not on the Chrome Web Store and was downloaded from an attacker-controlled server at oskeysetup[.]com, requiring manual sideloading using Developer Mode.

💡 Why it matters

  • Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.
  • If an organization thinks it might have been compromised or has an urgent matter, it should contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

#Unit42 #ThreatIntel #Vishing #Com-affiliated #Cybersecurity

Source: Dialing for Data: Inside the Com’s High-Profile Heists

item.title: Broadcom Patches VMware vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by Chinese Group
item.description:
Broadcom Patches VMware vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by Chinese Group

Broadcom has released emergency security updates to fix a critical VMware vCenter Server authentication bypass vulnerability that Chinese-linked hackers have exploited in zero-day attacks since September 2026.

🧩 How it works

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, affects the VMware Directory Service in vCenter Server, a management platform used to manage VMware virtualized environments. According to Broadcom, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter Server to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access.

  • Successful exploitation allows attackers to obtain administrative access to vCenter, giving them control over the virtual machines managed by the server.
  • The vulnerability affects vCenter regardless of whether Enhanced Linked Mode is enabled.

Mandiant researchers documented that attackers exploit the flaw to create a remote authentication bypass, establishing an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local. Using this session, attackers can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp.

⚙️ Key details

  • Patch Availability: Broadcom patched the vulnerability on November 19 in VMSA-2026-0009. This update also fixes four other vulnerabilities affecting VMware SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows.
  • Affected Software: The advisory notes that users are affected if running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the VMSA. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.
  • Workarounds: Broadcom states there are no official workarounds for the vulnerabilities, although network restrictions and firewall controls can help reduce exposure.
  • Urgency: The company considers the vCenter vulnerability an emergency update, urging organizations to install patches as soon as possible.
Tool/Malware Function
SLIMSAVAGE Web shells deployed to maintain persistent access and scan for VMware systems
BONESAW Custom Golang exploitation tool used to exploit CVE-2026-123890 and steal the directory database
SAWSNAKE Enables “Golden SAML” attacks to forge authentication tokens and bypass MFA
CAGEMATCH Web shell/backdoor used to execute commands and transfer files
BEARBONES Web shell/backdoor used to execute commands and steal credentials
LAZYBONES Web shell/backdoor used to execute commands and maintain access

🚨 Attack Context

Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group revealed that a suspected Chinese state-sponsored hacking group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-123890 in early September 2026. The VMware exploitation was part of the same intrusion campaign, where attackers first compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances (exploiting zero-day CVE-2026-102764) before moving laterally into internal Linux systems.

After gaining access to an internal Linux appliance, the hackers deployed SLIMSAVAGE web shells, escalated privileges to root, and scanned the internal network. They then used BONESAW to compromise a VMware vCenter Server. BONESAW creates a vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) administrator account and steals the server’s directory database. It can also extract SAML signing keys, allowing attackers to forge authentication tokens. Following exploitation, attackers deployed SAWSNAKE and additional backdoors to move deeper into virtualized environments, access ESXi hosts, and extract sensitive information, including Windows Active Directory database files.

💡 Why it matters

Mandiant says the use of two zero-day vulnerabilities in the same campaign, along with multiple malware families tailored to the targeted platforms, demonstrates the threat actor’s technical expertise. Researchers urge admins to apply the VMware security updates as soon as possible and configure additional security controls to protect their virtualization infrastructure.

#VMware #Broadcom #CVE-2026-123890 #ArmoryCastle #ZeroDay #InfoSec

Source: VMware patches vCenter zero-day exploited in attacks since September

item.title: How AWS Security Incident Response triages threat findings from GuardDuty
item.description:
How AWS Security Incident Response triages threat findings from GuardDuty

AWS Security Incident Response continuously triages threat findings from Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub CSPM, a process where most work never surfaces as a customer-facing case. The service ingests these findings through Amazon EventBridge rules automatically deployed during onboarding, ensuring that active threats are evaluated while posture and compliance issues remain in existing remediation processes.

🧩 How it works

The automated triage process evaluates each finding payload against several data sources to determine if an activity is benign or requires action.

  • Data sources: The service assesses the finding payload, related AWS activity from AWS CloudTrail and Amazon VPC Flow Logs, AWS threat intelligence, and user-provided environment context.
  • Benchmarking: Findings are mapped against a profile of known-good activity specific to the customer’s environment.
  • Third-party integration: Findings from tools like CrowdStrike, Trend Micro, or Lacework sent to Security Hub CSPM are also ingested, provided they carry complete payload information including resource ID, account ID, timestamp, and threat details. GuardDuty findings are ingested directly to prevent duplication.

⚙️ Key details

Outcomes of the triage process vary depending on the nature of the finding. Posture and compliance findings, such as misconfigurations or failed benchmark checks, are not triaged as they reflect environment state rather than active threats. They remain current without archiving and do not generate cases.

For active threat findings, such as compromised credentials, cryptomining, or data exfiltration, the service determines one of three dispositions:

Disposition Trigger Condition Action Taken
Archived, no action needed Automated triage or engineer confirms activity is benign or expected Finding is archived in GuardDuty; no case is created and no customer contact is made
Proactive case opened Triage cannot confirm activity is benign Case is opened as “Unconfirmed Activity” or “Inappropriate/Unintended Activity”; incident response team is engaged; finding stays Current until resolved
Retained for review Posture-related findings (e.g., overly permissive policies) No case is created; finding remains Current without archiving

When a proactive case is opened, customers respond via the AWS Management Console under the Cases section, allowing direct communication, context sharing, and case resolution. For third-party findings ingested through Security Hub CSPM, the disposition logic mirrors GuardDuty, but the status changes from NEW to NOTIFIED when triage begins, moving to SUPPRESSED if cleared as benign.

💡 Why it matters

The service builds a profile of what is normal in your environment to distinguish between expected behavior and genuine threats. For example, if GuardDuty flags an “UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS” finding, the service checks if the external IP belongs to a known corporate VPN range. If the pattern is recognized, the finding is archived. If the IP is from a hosting provider with no prior association and the IAM role has never called from outside AWS, a proactive case is created for investigation. Across customers, less than 1 percent of ingested findings result in a customer-facing escalation.

#AWS #Security #GuardDuty #IncidentResponse #ThreatDetection

Source: How AWS Security Incident Response triages your security findings | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Ransomware Defense: Detecting Pre-Encryption Attack Stages
item.description:
Ransomware Defense: Detecting Pre-Encryption Attack Stages

Ransomware attacks rarely begin with the ransomware payload itself. Operators first need an initial foothold, and common entry paths include exploitation of vulnerable internet-facing systems, abuse of stolen credentials, and social engineering. By the time encryption occurs, the intrusion may already include credential theft, privilege escalation, defense evasion, recovery sabotage, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. In data-extortion attacks, encryption may never happen at all, as operators steal data and threaten to leak it without encrypting anything.

🚀 Initial Entry Paths

Attacker entry into environments typically occurs through three primary vectors:

  • Vulnerable Systems: Unpatched, externally accessible services provide a route into the environment.
  • Stolen Credentials: Compromised credentials allow attackers to enter through legitimate remote-access or cloud services.
  • Social Engineering: This path targets users and the processes surrounding identity and access.

Once attackers establish access, they use stolen credentials and legitimate administration tools to move through victim environments before deploying ransomware.

🔍 Pre-Encryption Detection Signals

Defenders need to detect behaviors that precede encryption, not only the encryptor itself. Five high-value signals deserve immediate attention when monitoring for suspicious post-compromise behavior:

Signal Description
Defense tampering Attempts to stop security services, modify protection agents, load vulnerable drivers, or clear event logs.
Privilege escalation and lateral movement Unexpected privileged accounts, remote-execution tools spreading across hosts, or unusual server-to-server remote access.
Data exfiltration Unusual outbound transfers from systems that do not normally upload large volumes of data.
Recovery sabotage Deletion of shadow copies, backup catalogs, or recovery options using tools such as vssadmin.exe, wbadmin.exe, or bcdedit.exe.
Pre-encryption file behavior Rapid file enumeration, repeated read-write-rename activity, and encryption-like changes across local or network locations.

⚙️ Layered Defense Strategy

Stopping ransomware is rarely about a single control. A comprehensive strategy requires reducing opportunities for initial compromise, detecting and containing malicious activity when they do occur, and having a reliable way to recover if systems or data are affected.

  • Prevention: Reducing unnecessary internet exposure, prioritizing patching of high-risk systems, strengthening identity and access controls, and protecting email and collaboration channels.
  • Detection and Response: Monitoring endpoints for suspicious post-compromise behavior provides a layer when preventive controls do not stop the initial intrusion. Endpoint protection, email security, and extended detection and response (XDR) tools can identify and contain malicious activity across endpoints, email, and the wider environment.
  • Recovery: Integrated backup and recovery provide the path to restoring affected systems and data. It is important to note that this layer does not undo data theft, a critical distinction in double-extortion attacks.

#Ransomware #Cybersecurity #ThreatDetection #DataExfiltration

Source: Five warning signs of ransomware breach before encryption or data theft

item.title: Hacker Uses AI Agent Platform Cairn to Breach Over 100 Websites
item.description:
Hacker Uses AI Agent Platform Cairn to Breach Over 100 Websites

A hacker breached more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that largely operated on their own, according to the AI security firm Norforge.

🔍 Overview

  • The attacks targeted companies in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japan.
  • Reuters identified victims that included John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.
  • Norforge described the attacker as the “most active” among the exposed Cairn instances it discovered.

🧩 How it works

  • Cairn is an open‑source AI platform that calls itself a “general‑purpose problem‑solving engine.”
  • Users define a start and end point for AI agents, which then document their progress as they move forward.
  • While designed for legitimate problem‑solving, Norforge notes that the same tool can be repurposed to orchestrate cyber‑attacks.
  • The hacker set “preferred intrusion tactics” in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, and successful breaches took about 23 hours.

⚙️ Key details

  • Scale: More than 100 compromised sites; over 20 exposed Cairn instances deemed “likely malicious.”
  • Human involvement: The AI agents carried out the attacks with little involvement from the human hacker.
  • Company responses:
    Company Reported impact
    John Deere No indication that sensitive information was accessed
    SharkNinja Breach affected a standalone site with product support information; threat contained
    Cummins Investigating a potential cyber‑attack on a website operated by a third‑party vendor
  • Norforge is working to have the malicious Cairn instances taken down.
  • Cairn’s creator, @le1xia0, stated the platform “was never a ‘hacking tool’” and that misuse is a human decision.

💡 Why it matters

  • The incidents illustrate how advanced AI tools can be weaponized to conduct large‑scale cyber‑attacks with minimal human direction.
  • As AI capabilities grow, the line between legitimate automation and malicious misuse becomes increasingly blurred, heightening concerns for cybersecurity professionals.

#AIagents #Cybersecurity #Cairn

Source: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents

item.title: SOCRadar Alerts Integration Brings External Threat Intel into Elastic Security
item.description:
SOCRadar Alerts Integration Brings External Threat Intel into Elastic Security

Your SOC runs on Elastic. Detections, logs, cases and dashboards all live in Kibana, and your analysts have built their muscle memory around it. Until now, external threat intelligence – alarms about the Surface, Deep and Dark Web, brand abuse or the external attack surface – arrived in a dedicated platform, were reviewed there, and then manually re‑keyed into the SIEM or case tool. The new SOCRadar Alerts integration (v0.1.0) eliminates that handoff.

🔎 Overview

  • The integration pulls SOCRadar alarms via the SOCRadar API on a configurable polling interval, with an initial historical look‑back to backfill recent alarms.
  • Each alarm arrives with severity, status, alarm type, sub‑type, affected asset, related entities and detailed information.
  • Alarm data is mapped to the Elastic Common Schema (ECS), so SOCRadar fields sit next to your other sources with consistent names.

🧩 How it works

  1. Polling – The integration queries the SOCRadar API on the schedule you set.
  2. Normalization – Incoming alarm fields are translated into ECS fields.
  3. Ingestion – Normalized alarm documents are stored in the same Elastic workspace used for internal telemetry.
  4. Visualization – A built‑in Kibana dashboard displays severity distribution, alarm categories, volume trends and recent incidents.
  5. Investigation – Analysts can pivot from a dashboard tile to the underlying alarm document, correlate it with endpoint or identity events, and open a case without leaving Kibana.

⚙️ Key details

  • Alarm attributes – Every alarm carries:
    • Severity
    • Status
    • Alarm type and sub‑type
    • Affected asset
    • Related entities
    • Detailed description
  • Analyst workflow – Search, filter and build rules on external alarms exactly as on internal telemetry; prioritize by severity across both.
  • Time saved – No manual copy‑paste between consoles; the external context that triggered the investigation is already in the case.
Attribute What it provides
Severity A severity level for prioritization
Status Current processing state of the alarm
Alarm type / sub‑type Classification of the finding
Affected asset The asset the alarm relates to
Related entities Additional objects linked to the alarm
Details Full description and context

🚀 Availability

  • The integration is listed in the Elastic integrations catalog. To enable it, open the catalog, search for SOCRadar, and add the SOCRadar Alerts integration with your SOCRadar API credentials and polling preferences.
  • If you are not yet a SOCRadar customer, or need help configuring the three integrations together, contact your SOCRadar customer success manager or request a demo.

💡 Why it matters

  • Unified workspace – External threat intelligence appears in the same Elastic Security workspace where analysts already work.
  • Reduced handoff – The costly manual step of re‑keying alarms is removed, eliminating bottlenecks caused by volume and lost context.
  • Actionable context – Each alarm includes the asset and related entities, so investigations start with concrete, validated information.
  • Continuous visibility – The built‑in Kibana dashboard gives immediate insight into spikes, such as a high‑severity “New Digital Asset Discovery” followed by an “Impersonating Domain” alarm, enabling rapid response.

#SOCRadar #ElasticSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #SIEM #ECS

Source: SOCRadar Alarms in Elastic | Investigate Threats Faster

item.title: AI Accelerates Vulnerability Disclosure and Exploitation, GTIG Finds
item.description:
AI Accelerates Vulnerability Disclosure and Exploitation, GTIG Finds

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) examined vulnerability disclosure and exploitation statistics to evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the vulnerability threat landscape.

🔍 Overview

  • The analysis covers January 1 2025 through August 31 2026.
  • GTIG uses its own Vulnerability Risk Ratings (not CVSS) and tracks exploitation consequences and in‑the‑wild exploitation.
  • AI‑assisted discovery produces proportionally fewer Low‑Risk findings, more Moderate‑Risk findings, and more Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

📈 Disclosure Growth

  • Vulnerability disclosures doubled:
    • 5,045 disclosed in January 2026.
    • 10,477 disclosed in July 2026.
    • 10,740 disclosed in August 2026 (peak).
  • High‑Risk disclosures surged 167 %:
    • 131 in January 2026 → 350 in August 2026 (3 % of all disclosures).
  • Baseline High‑Risk disclosures more than doubled across the broader software ecosystem:
    • ~65 /month in mid‑2025 → ~135 /month in mid‑2026.
  • Specific spikes:
    • 75 High‑Risk flaws added in April‑May 2026 from mass research on consumer router firmware.
    • 128 High‑Risk vulnerabilities in August 2026 from Oracle’s quarterly Critical Patch Update and Linux kernel network driver advisories (≈ 37 % of August High‑Risk total).
Month High‑Risk Disclosures
Jan 2026 131
Aug 2026 350

⚙️ Exploitation Trends

  • Average monthly exploited vulnerabilities rose from 10.5 (2025) to 18 (Jan‑Aug 2026).
  • Zero‑day exploitation increased from an average of 8 per month (2025) to 11 per month (Jan‑Aug 2026).
  • From Jan‑Aug 2026, GTIG recorded 141 distinct vulnerabilities that were both disclosed and exploited, surpassing the total of 127 for the entire year 2025.
  • Only 0.23 % of all disclosed vulnerabilities in 2026 (≈ 1 in 431) were ever observed in active exploitation.
  • Monthly exploitation counts can be influenced by vendor disclosure cycles and threat‑actor campaign spikes.

🛡️ Risk Implications

  • AI‑driven discovery is shifting the risk profile toward more Moderate‑Risk and RCE‑capable flaws.
  • High‑Risk vulnerabilities remain a small proportion of total disclosures but are growing rapidly.
  • Automated CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) assignment policies across open‑source ecosystems can inflate baseline figures.
  • Linux‑Kernel‑only descriptions generated ~5,000 CVEs (Jan‑Aug 2026) with zero observed in‑the‑wild zero‑day exploitation.

🚀 Recommendations

  • Organizations should move from unprioritized mass‑patching to threat‑intelligence‑driven triage.
  • Combine targeted edge‑defense with automated, agentic remediation to manage the faster discovery and exploitation velocity.
  • Monitor vendor disclosure cycles and threat‑actor activity to better anticipate exploitation spikes.

📅 Outlook

  • GTIG expects vulnerability discovery and exploitation to continue growing in the short to medium term.
  • Ongoing analysis will focus on growth velocity and emerging threat vectors across the AI/LLM operational stack.

#AI #VulnerabilityManagement #ThreatIntelligence #Cybersecurity

Source: Vulnerability Discovery and Exploitation Trends in the AI Era | Google Cloud Blog
